title: TA9-24059
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX (hereinafter the claimant), his wife, XXXXXXX and their daughter, XXXXXX, citizens of Hungary, seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA). The claimants' identities have been established through certified copies of the claimants' passports.1

The claimant alleges that, as a Roma in Hungary, he will be discriminated against, harassed and even harmed simply because of his race. The discrimination is felt on many levels including in employment, education, housing, and in the general public.

The claimant is a 54-year-old male; he alleged that he and his family have experienced many years of racial hatred in his country because of their Romani ethnicity. He also alleged that, on XXXXXX 2003, he and his wife were on their way home when a car with several racists deliberately ran him over; fortunately, his wife fell in a ditch and was unharmed, but the claimant suffered multiple injuries. He was transported by ambulance to the hospital where he spent four days.

He alleged that on XXXXXXX, 2009, his son was coming home from school when he was attacked and beaten by a group of hooded men; four days later, their house was attacked. The attackers broke the entrance door and threatened the occupants. The claimant alleged that he and his family fled their home and stayed for a while with friends and relatives.

He alleged that the incidents were reported to the police, but they did not provide any protection; he felt that their lives were in danger, so on XXXXXXX, 2009, he and his wife fled his country to save their lives and filed for refugee status on the same day; their daughter left Hungary on XXXXXXX, 2010 and joined their claim.

The panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution for a Convention ground, or that he would personally be subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to his country. Therefore, the panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. Counsel's Written Submissions:

Counsel was given time to present written submissions which should have been received at the Board on or before December 21, 2011. At the time of writing this reason - January 20, 2012 - the submissions have not been received. ANALYSIS Credibility

With regard to credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal, which has ruled that testimony given under oath is presumed to be true, unless there is a valid reason to doubt its truthfulness.2 The assessment the panel must use to test the truth of a story of a witness is that it be in harmony with the preponderance of probabilities, which a practical and informed person would readily recognize as reasonable in that place and in those conditions.3 Furthermore, the panel cannot be satisfied that, "the evidence is credible or trustworthy unless satisfied that it is probably so, not just possibly so."4

The panel, in considering the credibility of the claimant, made an assessment of all the evidence, both oral and documentary.5 The evidence was also assessed as a whole so it could be treated in a consistent manner.6 However, not every piece of evidence will be referred to, but those the panel finds relevant to its decision.7 Even if a piece of evidence is not referred to, the panel carefully considered it as part of the evidence.8 The panel is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibility, common sense and rationality, and may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole.

The claimant testified that, on XXXXXXX 2003, he was deliberately struck by a car, which was driven by a group of racists as he and his wife were walking on their way home from the grocery store. He testified that the occupants of the car, realizing that they were Romani, at first followed them with the car while shouting racial slurs at them. Just before the car ran the claimant over, the occupants shouted to the claimant and his wife that they were going to die. The claimant was severely injured and was transported by ambulance to the hospital where he remained for four days, after which he was released and sent home.9

Noting that this information was very central to the claimant's claim but it was not included in the port of entry (POE) notes10 or in the original Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative11 but was submitted as an amendment to the PIF narrative on December 2, 2011, he was asked why the information was not included in his application for refugee status; he replied that, when they arrived in Canada, he did not know what was happening to them. He said to come from such a tiny country to a large country he felt completely lost at the airport. He said it was afterward it became clear to him that they had to write a story. He said their arrival to Canada was very simple; they were treated nicely, so they were happy and felt that they got away from the bad things.

The claimant was therefore asked why then he did not mention the incident in his original narrative; he replied that it was after the fact they were told that the information was foundational; then they paid attention to the matter. He said back then they were not able to, and they were told that the information they wrote down was sufficient. The panel finds the claimant's explanation unreasonable and rejects it. For example, it was pointed out to the claimant that the information about this incident was very important, yet he never mentioned it; he replied that, when he arrived at the airport, he was asked about personal data; he said the conversation did not go beyond that; they did ask him why they had come to Canada; he said that was all. The claimant was asked, "when you were asked why you came to Canada, why did not you tell them about the incident"; he replied, honestly we were not aware what was happening to us. He added that it took them several weeks to understand what was happening to them. In fact, claimant testified that the story they had originally written was about their children, but after they changed lawyers, he showed the lawyer that he had the papers,12 which is why they amended the narrative. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that if the story about being intentionally run over by a group of racists was credible, he would have remembered it and included it in his original story despite his testimony that he was on medication and is often forgetful. For example, the claimant was able to remember several other incidences even though he was on medication and is often forgetful.

The panel therefore finds that, even though the incident occurred over 8 years ago, because of the allegation that he was deliberately ran over by a group of racists in a car who threatened to kill him and his wife and the fact that he continues to experienced medical problems from this blatant attempt on his and his wife's lives and given the seriousness of the allegation, if indeed the allegation is not an embellishment, on a balance of probabilities, he would have included it in his application for refugee status. The Court has said that a person's first account of events is usually more reliable and must be considered more trustworthy.13 The panel therefore finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the incident was an accident; the claimant belatedly thought to use the incident to embellish his story to enhance his claim for refugee status, which undermines his credibility.

The panel notes that, when the female claimant was asked why they did not mention this incident in their application for refugee status and their original PIF narrative, she replied that they did not know that they had to tell them about it. She said that they (she and her husband) were "dumb people, unfortunately we are uneducated." What was written in the POE notes was read to the female claimant; she said that was correct. It was pointed out to her that they were able to say all these things but nothing about the incident; at this point, she replied that they did not know that it was an important thing; and she added, we say it from the bottom of our hearts. The panel finds her explanation unreasonable. The panel does not believe that being run down by a car with a bunch of racists would not be considered important to include in a claim based on persecution because of their race - it makes no sense.

While the panel takes into account the claimant's level of education-8 years14-and believes that she may very well be unsophisticated, but in watching and listening to her give testimony, she is intelligent. The panel therefore finds, on a balance of probabilities, that what happened to her and her husband on XXXXXXX 2003 was an accident, pure and simple, which is why it was not mentioned in the POE notes and original PIF narrative. At the same time, the panel is aware of the pitfalls in relying on port-of-entry notes, as outlined in the case of Nowa,15 with regard to omissions and contradictions as not always being the basis for an adverse credibility finding.

Therefore, additional evidence was gleaned. For example, an excerpt from the medical report was read to the female claimant that spoke of the incident as an accident: "Patient suffered a car accident in 2003." Also, the panel notes that, "Patient says that he has been feeling worse since his accident".16 She was asked if she could explain why it was written as an accident; she replied that she did not know why it was written like that. She then reiterated that her husband was run over by a car. The panel, maintaining its finding that it was an accident, also notes that when she was asked if she told the doctor that her husband was run over by a car; she said, "Yes, we told them everything."

The panel reminds itself that, according to documentary evidence before it, The Hungarian Helsinki Committee (HHC), a non-profit organization that monitors the enforcement of international human rights norms in Hungary, indicates in its correspondence with the Research Directorate that, according to the Act XLVII of 1997 on the Handling and Protection of Medical and Related Personal Data, a doctor "shall immediately report" patient's personal information (name, gender, place and date of birth, mother's name, place of residence and social security number) to the police if the patient suffered a serious bodily harm "presumably as a consequence of a crime. Whether doctors are obligated to report serious or crime-related injuries; requirements and procedures to obtain medical reports within Hungary, including who can obtain them; whether they can be obtained from abroad, including requirements and procedures. The HHC notes that Act CLIV of 1997 on Health does not mention the reporting of crimes among the responsibilities of the medical staff.17

The panel therefore finds, on a balance of probabilities, that if the claimants had reported to the doctor/s that a crime had taken place, as she testified that that they did, the doctor/s would have immediately reported it to the police as is required. The panel notes that the claimant testified that his wife reported the incident to the police the next day, which means that it was not a crime as the doctor/s would have done so immediately when they became aware that a crime was committed. As such, while the panel believes that the claimant was run over by a car,18 it believes it was accidentally done, and it rejects their allegation that the car was driven by a group of racists that intentionally ran him over and further finds that it undermines their credibility. At the same time, the panel notes that, when he was asked if he had a police report of the incident, he replied, they never ever written a police report. He also testified that the police never looked him up meaning that they never asked about him at the hospital and never came to his home.

Given the serious problems with respect to major issues, the panel finds that the claimant was generally lacking in credibility. It simply does not believe that, on a balance of probabilities, any of the significant events that the claimant alleged happened to him, actually happened. Discrimination vs. Persecution

The claimant testified that he left his country because of racial hatred he experienced for many years. He said that at school his children were placed in a separate class from other Hungarian children; they were humiliated as well. As a result, his children did not receive the education they should and were treated as mentally challenged; because of that, they were branded and were not accepted at higher educational institutions. He testified that his children were called names, such as "stinking lice-infested Gypsies". He stated that, as racial hatred increased against Roma, they did not have steady places to work as nobody hired them; when they were hired, in times of layoffs, they were the first to go. He declared that the current regime punishes and blames Roma for everything. He said that the Jobbik Party and the Hungarian Guards organized attacks against Roma, killing Roma children. At night houses of Roma are firebombed with Molotov cocktails and stoned.

The claimant testified that, on XXXXXXX, 2009, his son was attacked and beaten as he was coming home from school by a group of men. Four days later, his house was attacked and they were threatened; this forced them to leave their home to stay with friends and relatives for a while. The claimant also testified that a group of racists travelling in a car ran him over. Although the incidents were reported to the police, they did nothing. Fearing for their lives and safety, he fled his country and came to Canada.

The panel agrees that the claimant may have suffered discrimination but finds no persuasive evidence that he had been mistreated by the medical system in Hungary. He presented no corroborative evidence to support any allegations of discrimination in education, work, medical care, etc. The panel finds that, on a balance of probabilities, none of the incidents mentioned indicate that the claimant has been denied adequate medical care in Hungary because of his ethnicity. The evidence is that he received medical treatment whenever he sought it. For example, the claimant was transported to hospital by ambulance where he remained for four days; he testified that when he was placed in the hospital room, Hungarian patients were upset that he was sharing the room. He said that, the following day, the other patients were moved out, and he was alone in the big room. Based on the extent of the injuries, the claimant did not believe that he should have been released from the hospital so soon; he also testified that, while in the hospital, he had requested painkiller medication, but it was denied, and he attributes all of this to his ethnicity.

Based on the various documentations perused by the panel, the panel reaffirms that there may have been discrimination against the claimant in Hungary because of their ethnicity, but does the discrimination suffered by him amount to persecution when considered singularly or cumulatively? To be considered persecution, the mistreatment suffered or anticipated must be serious. In order to determine whether a particular mistreatment would qualify as "serious", one must examine what interest of the claimant might be harmed and to what extent the subsistence, enjoyment, expression or exercise of that interest might be compromised. "Persecution", for example, undefined in the Convention, has been ascribed the meaning of sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection.19 In the case of Chan,20 La Forest J. (in dissent) reiterated that the essential question is whether the persecution alleged by the claimant threatens his or her basic human rights in a fundamental way.

There is no persuasive evidence that the claimant was persecuted in education, employment, housing or medical care in Hungary. At the same time, the panel notes that Human rights non-government organizations (NGOs) reported that Roma were discriminated against in almost all fields of life, particularly in employment, education, housing, penal institutions, and access to public places, such as restaurants and bars. According to statistics of the Hungarian Institute for Educational Research and Development, Roma were significantly less educated than other citizens, with incomes and life expectancy well below average.21

The physical attacks on the claimant are considered in the following section on state protection. The conclusion reached was that there was no persuasive evidence of a sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights of the claimant, demonstrative of a failure of state protection.
The panel has also considered these matters cumulatively and finds that they do not rise to the level of persecution. State Protection

According to the Central Statistics Office, in 2007 the Romani community was the largest ethnic minority, accounting for 2% of the population, or about 200,000 persons. However, unofficial estimates, which vary widely, suggest the actual figure was much higher, ranging from between 500,000 and 800,000 persons. Violent attacks against Roma continued and generated strong public concern and intense disputes as to the existence of racially motivated crime in the country. Human rights NGOs reported that Roma were discriminated against in almost all fields of life, particularly in employment, education, housing, penal institutions, and access to public places, such as restaurants and bars.

According to the statistics of the Hungarian Institute for Educational Research and Development, Roma were significantly less educated than other citizens, and their incomes and life expectancy were well below average. A 2007 International Labour Organization report estimated the unemployment rate among Roma to be 40%. However, in many underdeveloped regions of the country, it exceeded 90%. Romani unemployment was estimated to be three to five times higher than among the non-Romani population. Inadequate housing continued to be a problem for Roma; their overall living conditions remained significantly worse than the general population's. The attitude of some Hungarian people, including some in positions of authority, toward the Roma is certainly discriminatory and prejudicial. It is clear from the documentary evidence that the effect has been to marginalize the Roma people. Roma are generally under-employed, under-educated, frequently live in subsistence housing, and are now subject to violence from radical elements who are gaining support from the general public to some extent. It is against this background, and in taking into consideration the particular circumstances relating to this claim, that the panel must determine whether or not adequate state protection exists for this particular claimant in Hungary.

The determinative issue in the case at hand is the presumption that countries are capable of protecting its citizens, and this underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" confirmation of the state's inability to protect its citizens.22 A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is in fact, inadequate. The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.23

In view of these principles, the panel finds that the claimant has not provided the requisite clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in Hungary is inadequate.

The claimant was questioned as to what efforts he made to seek state protection before fleeing Hungary. First, the panel notes that the claimant was very evasive in some of his answers. For example, he was asked if the police investigated the incident (accident of XXXXX, 2003); he replied that his wife went to the police station - she should be the one to tell the panel what she was told when she went there. The question was repeated (did the police investigate the incident); he replied, when a Roma person goes to the police station, they are laughed at; the police say in a derogatory way to go home, and they will look into it; but they do nothing more. The panel asked the question the third time, did the police investigate the incident? He replied, "The police did not take steps - we did go to report it to them". The panel finds his evasiveness to straightforward questions to undermine his credibility and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that he had difficulties answering the questions because his report was taken by the police and the accident investigated.

However, the panel notes that, even if the police did not take his report and did not investigate his complaint, he was asked if he was satisfied with the police response to his complaint; he replied, "how can I be when we do not have safety; we did not receive any protection." Since, according to his testimony, the police did not help, he was asked if he reported the conduct of the police to any other authority. The claimant replied that he had no knowledge of any higher authority; he said the police are responsible to protect the citizens. Asked if he went to any other authority to report the police inaction to his complaint, he replied that, in Hungary, the Gypsies are so oppressed they are not given any right of appeal; even if they report it, they let it drag on until it is forgotten. "So you did not report the police conduct?" He replied, we cannot report it; there is no such place to report it. However, later he said that there was one place - the Minister - but that is in Budapest which is 240 KM away. The panel notes that he came all the way to Canada from Hungary to seek international protection but thought travelling 240 KM was too far to go to get help - it makes no sense to this panel.

The claimant is responsible to exhaust all available means domestically before leaping into the international arena. He said the police did not help him, but local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.24 Therefore, if the police did not help because of corruption, racism, etc., he is still required to seek state protection in his country.

According to documentary evidence, the claimant has help available: Anyone may turn to the Minorities Commissioner with a complaint and request that an irregularity concerning national and ethnic minority rights be investigated either in their own case or on behalf of their community, for instance, if they have experienced negative discrimination due to their background. His (the Minorities Commissioner) task is to monitor the enforcement of national and ethnic minority rights. As the monitoring body of Parliament, the Minorities Ombudsman examines whether the processes of the authorities and public service providers, including the police, comply with the requirements of constitutionality and legality. The Minorities Commissioner may also take action if he becomes aware of unjust procedures or negative discrimination.25

The panel prefers the documentary evidence over the claimant's testimony since they are drawn from a wide range of publicly accessible documents, from reliable non-government and government organizations.

The claimant testified that his son, who is not before the panel, was attacked and physically assaulted on XXXXXX, 2009 by a group of hooded men. This is the only other case of physical assault against his family and which occurred about six years after his accident on XXXXX, 3003. However, he testified that, four days hence, his house was attacked when a group of intruders smashed widows and broke down a door causing them to flee. Fearful to return, they stayed with friends and relatives for a while. The claimant testified that, a couple of days later, they reported the incident to the police "word for word." He, however, testified that the police did not record his complaint.

The panel notes that the claimants testified that the police did not take any of their reports - XXXX 2004 and XXXXXX 2009 - but there was no follow-up to any of these complaints, or were the behaviour of the police officers reported to any higher or other authority, especially as he did not consider the Minority Government, which he approached, as an "authority." Not only is protection offered by police agencies to be considered but other state agencies as well.26 Protection can be provided not just by state-run agencies such as the police but also by non-governmental agencies which receive state funding.27 Some Federal Court decisions, however, hold a contrary view.28 The panel however notes that some Federal Court decisions have expressed reservations in this regard, however, stating that it is the police force that has the primary responsibility to protect a nation's citizens and, unless there is evidence to the contrary, alternative institutions do not constitute avenues of protection per se.

Documentary evidence before the panel states: The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Rights of National and Ethnic Minorities, also referred to as the Minorities Ombudsman, noted in correspondence with the Research Directorate that the Police Act of 1994 allows for a complaint against the "unlawful action" of a police officer to be submitted to the local captain of the police, with a higher ranking captain having the option to appeal the decision (Hungary 19 Sept. 2011). The resulting decision can be reviewed by the court. In correspondence with the Research Directorate, the HHC similarly noted that the Police Act allows for any individual who has his or her "fundamental" rights violated by the police to "file a complaint with the police unit responsible" for the violation.

The panel notes that, since the incident of XXXX 2004 (and the panel believes it was an accident and not intentional), there was no further incident of physical violence against the claimant and his family until XXXXXX, 2004, followed by an attack on their home four days later. There is therefore no persuasive evidence before this panel that, even if these incidents did occur, they were not random. The panel notes that the Court said that random assaults where the assailants are unknown to the victim and there are no independent witnesses are difficult to effectively investigate and protect against. In all such circumstances, even the most effective, well-resourced and highly motivated police forces will have difficulty providing effective protection. This Court should not impose on other states a standard of "effective" protection that police forces in our own country, regrettably, sometimes only aspire to.29

But even if the incidents were not random, there is no persuasive evidence before this panel that the police were not investigating the complaints and were not making meaningful efforts to apprehend the perpetrators. For example, there is no evidence that the police told the claimants that they would not investigate their complaints; there was no evidence that the police were abusive to them. In fact, with respect to the accident, the female claimant testified that the police told her that they were going to look into the matter and notify them, even though she claimed, "but nothing happened." However, when she was asked, did you go back to the police and ask about the status of the investigation, she replied that she did not go back. Asked why she did not go back to the police to see about the status of the investigation, she replied that it never crossed her mind to go back because she was busy with her husband in the hospital. The panel finds that it is their responsibility to exhaust all reasonable available means domestically to obtain state protection before they seek international protection.

Also, the claimant testified that when his son was attacked and assaulted, they reported it to the police. Asked if the police took a report, he said no. He testified that the police explained that because the claimant could not identify the attackers (the attackers wore masks), there was not anything the police could do. With respect to the attack on their apartment, the claimant testified that he also made a report to the police. However, the claimant testified that, during the home invasion, they hid in a cool-storage room which saved them. When he was asked how he knew that the attackers were Guardists, the panel notes that he did not say he saw them; he replied that only the Guardists do those things. The panel therefore finds his explanation speculative that his home was attacked by Guardists. As such, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that their complaints were investigated despite the limited information with which to work. The panel reminds itself that local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.30 For example, the Court has stated that, when the agent of persecution is not the state, the lack of state protection had to be assessed as a matter of state capacity to provide protection rather than from the perspective of the effectiveness of local apparatus in providing protection in a given circumstance. Thus, in the absence of evidence pointing to a more general policy by which the state's protection is not extended to the target group, a refusal to provide protection at the local level does not constitute a refusal to provide protection.31

While the panel notes that according to documentary evidence before it a variety of sources indicate that police corruption in Hungary is a problem; two sources state that Hungarian police officers are susceptible to corruption32 and that, even though Hungary has one of the most advanced anti-discrimination laws and a system for minority protection in the Central and Eastern European region and a number of mechanisms have been developed to ensure that minority groups enjoy civil and political rights, it is said that the central government has generally failed to maintain strong and effective control mechanisms over rights violations against Hungary's largest minority, the Roma. For example, Roma victims face very often discriminatory treatment by the police: officers are reluctant to register their reports and especially the racial motivation of a crime reported. A September 2010 shadow report, prepared for the UN Human Rights Committee by the Legal Defence Bureau for National and Ethnic Minorities (NEKI), Minority Rights Group International (MRG) and the Serbian Institute of Budapest, also states that complaints submitted to NEKI "show that the Roma minority still experience[s] discrimination by the police during investigations and criminal proceedings." Roma victims often experience discriminatory treatment (lack of information and legal help, reluctance from the police etc.) by the police from the very first moment when they want to report a crime. This problem is the most tangible in hate crime investigations where Roma are the victims of serious racially motivated crimes. Also, it is noted that on anti-Roma violence in Hungary, the police showed efforts in bringing perpetrators of "high-profile" crimes to justice, especially crimes reported in the media.33 Police response to complaints lodged by Roma citizens; procedures to lodge a complaint against a police officer; alternate complaints mechanisms for human rights violations).

The panel notes that the crimes against the claimants may not have been considered high profile and would not necessarily receive the same response akin to those considered high profile; however, the panel believes that, in the absence of any persuasive evidence, these claimants did not and could not receive state protection.

The panel found the claimant's responses regarding the effectiveness of state protection were not persuasive, since they were not credible and were largely unsubstantiated and were not consistent with the documentary evidence.

The panel however would be remiss if it did not acknowledge and consider that there is information in the documentation to indicate that there is widespread reporting of incidents of intolerance, discrimination and persecution of Romani individuals in Hungary. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that Hungary candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the treatment of minorities in that country, especially in the case of the Roma. The panel recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in Hungary for Roma who are victims of crime, police abuse, discrimination or persecution, that Hungary is making serious efforts to address these problems, and that the police and government officials are both willing and able to protect victims.

There is considerable activism in Hungary by the country's ethnic minorities for the protection of their rights. In July 1993 the government adopted legislation guaranteeing the cultural, civil and political rights of 12 minority groups and prohibiting ethnic discrimination. Following the approval of this legislation, minority rights activists launched a new campaign to change Hungary's electoral law, with the aim of securing the direct representation of ethnic groups in the legislature. In the 1994 municipal elections, ethnic minorities were able to elect their own local ethnic authorities, with consultative roles on cultural and educational issues affecting the community. In February 1995, Hungary signed the counsel of Europe Convention on the Protection of National Minorities. In April, the Roma of Hungary elected their own governing body, the National Autonomous Authority of the Romany minority, which was in power to administer funds and deliberate issues affecting the Roma. In December 2008, the Metropolitan Court in Budapest ordered the dissolution of the extreme nationalist Hungarian Guard, which was responsible for attacks and discriminatory behaviour against the Roma community. A court of appeal upheld the ruling, stating that the organization incited violence and violated the freedom of others. This prohibition was confirmed by the Supreme Court in December, 2008.34

The National Police Headquarters (NPH), which operates under the direction of the Ministry of Interior, is responsible for enforcing laws and maintaining order nationwide. Twenty regional police departments are directly subordinate to the NPH; city police are subordinate to the regional police and have local jurisdiction.

Penalties for police officers found guilty of wrongdoing include reprimand, dismissal, and criminal prosecution. A legislative amendment that took effect on March 24 mandates the automatic dismissal of police officers convicted of criminal acts committed while on duty.
Victims of lesser police abuses may complain either to the alleged violator's unit or to the Independent Police Complaints Board (IPCB).

In the first 10 months of the year, authorities found 2,914 police officers responsible for breaches of discipline, 868 guilty of petty offences, 310 guilty of criminal offences, and eight unfit for duty.

In the same period, courts sentenced seven police officers to prison terms, gave suspended sentences to 25, fined 315, demoted four, and dismissed 11. In the same period, courts convicted 32 officers of corruption. No information was available on the number placed on probation.

The IPCB, established in 2008, investigated violations and omissions by the police that affected fundamental rights. The five-member body, appointed by a two-thirds majority of the National Assembly, functions independently of police authorities. As of December 8, the Board had received 285 complaints from the public. It reviewed 501 (including some cases filed in 2009) and found legal violations in 157. The Board forwarded the 157 cases to the national police chief, who agreed with the findings in one case, partially accepted the findings in 27, and rejected the remainder. The IPCB's authority is limited to making recommendations to the NPH and reporting its findings to Parliament.35

The expansion of the Roma Anti-Discrimination Customer Service Network means that in 2008 there were 30 lawyers at 47 municipalities in the country, and the coordination of the program in the Ministry is ensured by a desk officer for Roma affairs. Clients can obtain information on the customer service contact details of network lawyers 24 hours a day. There was a nation-wide campaign promoting the network and toll-free number. Since 2004 the Network has handled more than 7,200 cases.36

There is also recourse to the Equal Treatment Authority. Since 2005 it has provided individuals with a direct avenue of redress for violations of the prohibition of discrimination in a variety of public and private law relationships. In the first year, there were nearly 500 complaints lodged and the number has risen steadily every since. There are also other remedies such as seeking compensation through the courts, or turning to one of the Parliamentary Commissioners where public authorities are concerned.37

There is also the Roma Police Officers' Association in Hungary and Roma are able to file a complaint to the association. The complaints mostly concern discrimination in employment, discriminatory treatment, and discrimination by law enforcement authorities or police officers.38
If the claimant faces discrimination, she has recourse to all these programs for assistance should she need it.

The Hungarian government has taken a number of legal and institutional measures to improve the situation of the Romani minority. According to the open Society Institute, Hungary has one of the most advanced systems for minority protection in the region. The Hungarian Government lists a number of institutions within the state apparatus, including the Roma Integration Department within the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labor, the main government body responsible for Romani integration and the Council of Roma Integration, a consultative, advisory body, which coordinates measures between various ministries on the social inclusion of Roma.39 Hungary has taken a number of initiatives relating to the situation of the Roma including, education, employment, housing, health, and political representation.40

Hungary faces criticism regarding the implementation of the laws that it has enacted to address the discrimination and persecution of its minorities, especially the Romani. While there may be motivation within the central government to have its laws enforced, there is difficulty in implementing the enforcement of these laws at the local level, and resources routinely fail to reach the groups with the greatest needs. The criticism against Hungary may be deserved, but what is important to note is that Hungary is a part of the European Union and is therefore responsible for upholding a number of various standards to maintain its membership in the Union. For instance, the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance (ECRI) was established by the Council of Europe. It is an independent human rights monitoring body specializing in questions relating to racism and intolerance. It is composed of independent and impartial members, who are appointed on the basis of their moral authority and recognized expertise in dealing with racism, xenophobia, anti-Semitism and intolerance. The ECRI published a report on Hungary in which it gives praise to Hungary for its accomplishments, cites issues of concern, and gives recommendation for future action.41

What is important to note in this instance is that Hungary is not an island unto its own, but it is a responsible member of the European Union and reports regularly to the governance structures within that Union. Even if criticism of Hungary's measures to combat racism is warranted, particularly against the Romani population, on a balance of probabilities, Hungary is taking the measures to implement the standards that are mandated as a member of the European Union.

Therefore, having considered the totality of the evidence, the panel find that the claimant, in the circumstances of this case, has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and that the claimant did not take all reasonable steps in the circumstances to avail herself of that protection before making a claim for refugee protection. Therefore, the panel is not persuaded that the state of Hungary would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimant seek it.

There is no persuasive evidence before the panel that the claimant would face persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, face a risk to her life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture, if she returned to Hungary.

For all of these reasons, the panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the Act, as state protection is available to him. Principles and Jurisprudence Applied
In the case at hand, the panel has applied the following principles and jurisprudence.

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by the jurisprudence from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection, and the panel has applied those principles to the case at hand.

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. Having canvassed the country conditions documents, the panel finds that Hungary is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country.42

To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" confirmation of the state's inability to protect its citizens.43 A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is, in fact, inadequate. The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.44 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection.45 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.46 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.47

Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection to be invoked only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of their home state. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.48 To qualify for refugee status, a claimant must satisfy the Board that he or she sought, but was unable to obtain, protection from their home state, or, alternatively, that their home state, on an objective basis, could not be expected to provide protection.49 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.50

A claimant's burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in question: the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them.51 In a functioning democracy, a claimant will have a heavy burden when attempting to show that they should not have been required to exhaust all of the recourses available to them domestically before claiming refugee status.52

The documentary evidence53 before the Board indicates that Hungary is a democracy, and there are free and fair elections. There is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary. Therefore, in countries such as Hungary, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.54

Local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.55

No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.56 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.57 CONCLUSION

The panel determines that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim. Since the claims of the other claimants rest on the same set of facts, their claims also failed. (signed) "Edward C. Robinson" Edward C.
